source.title: Open Problems on Information and Feedback Controlled Systems

accepted.question_text: In a feedback-controlled system, a controller measures the system state and chooses control actions using that information rather than acting independently of the state. What general upper bounds can be proved for how much the system's performance can increase when the controller has a specified amount of information about the system state? Here, performance means quantities such as work output, efficiency, flux, or power, and the question asks for bounds that quantify the maximum improvement achievable from information-driven feedback over comparable open-loop control.

evidence.quote: Controllers are called closed-loop or feedback controllers if their actions are dependent on the state of the system and called open-loop if otherwise.
Therefore, the first natural main question is how much the performance can be increased with a certain amount of information, or, stated otherwise, which are the bounds of the performance increase.

accepted.question_text: For feedback-controlled systems in which information is transferred from the system to a controller and then used to choose actions, what is the correct thermodynamic theory that fully accounts for the thermodynamic effects of that information transfer? In particular, how should one formulate the thermodynamic relations and resulting limits, such as bounds on extractable work and efficiency, for closed-loop control processes that use information about the system state?

evidence.quote: The second main question is the establishment of the thermodynamics of feedback controlled systems accounting for thermodynamic effects of the information transfer.

This second question can be seen as included in the first one, as, for instance, the computation of the maximum efficiency involves a bound in the work that can be extracted from the feedback controlled system.

accepted.question_text: Consider a feedback-controlled system undergoing correlated repeated actuation, meaning that the controller measures and actuates repeatedly before the system has relaxed to equilibrium, so successive controller actions contain redundant information. What is the precise relation between the entropy-reduction formulas derived from the point of view of the controlled system for such correlated repeated feedback and Zurek's algorithmic-complexity approach, which analyzes the combined system-plus-controller and derives the minimum energetic cost of erasing the controller's stored measurement record?

evidence.quote: Correlated repeated actuation of the feedback controller is present when the controller repeatedly actuates the system without waiting for the relaxation of the system to equilibrium between actuations.

One particular open question involves the precise relations between these recent results and the algorithmic complexity approach adopted by Zurek [6, 7] to study the correlated repeated actuation of a feedback controller from the perspective of the system plus controller.
This study has allowed Zurek to establish the minimum energetic cost for erasing a memory that has stored the measurements the controller has processed

accepted.question_text: For feedback-controlled systems with repeated feedback actuation, can the entropy-reduction results already obtained for correlated repeated control be applied or extended to derive rigorous bounds for additional performance measures, especially the maximum attainable flux and the maximum attainable power?

evidence.quote: Another open question is the application or the extension of the results found in [13] to find bounds for other performance measures of feedback controlled systems, for example, the maximum attainable flux or power.

accepted.question_text: When a feedback controller actuates so frequently that its actuation period is shorter than any characteristic time scale of the system dynamics, the control becomes effectively continuous and is a limiting case of correlated repeated feedback. How can the entropy and information results proved for discrete repeated feedback control be extended to this continuous-actuation limit, despite the nontrivial relationship between discrete entropy and differential entropy?

evidence.quote: Continuous actuation of the feedback controller is effectively present when the controller repeatedly actuates on the system with a period shorter than any of the characteristic time scales of the system dynamics.
However, the continuous time limit of the results found in [13] is not direct because of the nontrivial relationship between differential entropy and discrete entropy
Therefore, even the extension of the results in [13] to the continuous actuation limit remains still an open problem.

accepted.question_text: Feedback-controlled flashing ratchets are stochastic systems in which a controller uses information about the system state to switch a ratchet potential on and off and thereby rectify thermal fluctuations. How can the general entropy-reduction and thermodynamic results already obtained for feedback-controlled systems be applied to feedback-controlled flashing ratchets so as to establish bounds on the attainable entropy reduction and to formulate the thermodynamics of these ratchets?

evidence.quote: These feedback controlled ratchets can improve the performance over its open-loop counterparts thanks to the information the controller gets about the system state.
The application of the results of [13] to feedback controlled flashing ratchets has not been done yet.
It will allow to establish bounds on the entropy reduction attainable for feedback flashing ratchet and to establish the thermodynamics of these systems

accepted.question_text: For feedback-controlled flashing ratchets, existing bounds on performance improvement were formulated in terms of the information gathered by the controller per actuation. How should those bounds be reformulated in terms of the total non-redundant information acquired per unit time, so that only genuinely new information is counted and the ratchet bounds can be related to the entropy-reduction and thermodynamic results for general repeated feedback control?

evidence.quote: These relation were stated in terms of the information per actuation.
However, how to restate these relations in terms of the total amount of information per unit time (i.e., only computing non-redundant information per unit time) is still an open question.
This restatement will help to put these results [38, 39] in relation with those found in [13] for the entropy reduction and the thermodynamics of a general feedback controlled system.

accepted.question_text: In nanotechnology devices and biological systems where one subsystem interacts bidirectionally with another and effectively acts as a controller that uses information to improve the other subsystem's performance, what concrete limitations on operation and performance follow from the general performance bounds for feedback-controlled systems? In other words, how do the theoretical limits for information-driven feedback translate into limits for such nanotechnological and biological systems?

evidence.quote: Thus, the bounds of the performance of the feedback controlled systems will imply limitations to the operation of nanotechnology devices and biological systems.
Finding these implications is still a very relevant open question.
